## Personality

Bright, theatrical and generous, she will sing for anyone who asks and many who do not.

## Lore

Lyra is the Singer of the Old Songs, and on any evening when it is not pouring with rain, you can find her somewhere on the Lantern Paths singing them. She is thirty-two, bright, theatrical and generous. She will sing for anyone who asks and for a great many people who do not, and she sings everything, from children's counting rhymes to the long, dark songs of the Balrog War, as if it were the most important song in the world and you were the only person she had ever wanted to sing it to.

### Where the songs came from

Lyra learned most of her songs from her grandfather, Aspen, the retired treewright. Her mother Fennel, Aspen's only child, had a fine voice too, and sang her to sleep with the old lullabies; Lyra's father, a travelling fiddler, died before she was old enough to remember him, and she has only a story or two about him and the tunes her mother said were his. When Lyra was ten, twenty-two years ago, Fennel died of a fever in a hard winter. Lyra went to live with Aspen and her grandmother Elda, and when Elda died four years later, it was Aspen alone who raised her.

Those were long evenings, and often neither of them could sleep. So Aspen sang. He knew the songs his own grandparents had sung, the songs the treewrights sang while they worked, the songs about the first Magicians and the Listening Woods, and the old war songs nobody sang at parties. He sang them all, badly and with great feeling, and Lyra learned every one. She says he saved her life with them, and Aspen, who is talkative about everything else, goes quiet when she says it.

He still comes to hear her nearly every evening and sits as close to the front as he can. He also corrects her when she changes a word, and she changes one now and then just to watch him do it.

### The bridge by the tea house

On fine evenings Lyra sings on the branch-bridge outside the Dewdrop Tea House, so that the guests inside can hear her through the open windows. Tansy, who keeps the tea house, is one of her oldest friends. When Lyra first came to live on the Lantern Paths, a grieving ten-year-old, Tansy's mother Hollyn fed her honey cakes in the kitchen, and Tansy, then fourteen, let her stand on a chair in the tea room and sing to the guests. Lyra has been singing for the Dewdrop's guests ever since, and Tansy has never once let her pay for a cake. Lyra pays her back with songs, and with Liri, whom she has been teaching rhymes since the girl could talk.

### The war songs

Among the songs Lyra sings are the ones about the Balrog War: the First Burning, the truce, the long days at the foot of the World Tree, the Savage front line that held, and the Magicians who worked the seal. They are not cheerful songs. Lyra sings them anyway, every few evenings, because she thinks people ought to know them, and because lately she has noticed that people are listening to them differently. Travellers who have come in off the roads go very still during the war songs, and do not clap afterwards.

### The verses nobody remembers

Lyra is collecting the verses nobody else remembers. She asks every old person in the forest to sing her what they know, and writes down every verse that differs from Aspen's. She has found lullabies with extra lines, work songs with whole verses missing from the common versions, and a war song that three different old singers each knew a different ending to. Each spring, when the highland visitors come from Midbarium to see the Eldest, she trades songs with them, and has learned that some of the old war songs are sung in Midbarium too, with the same tunes and different words.

One fragment troubles her. It belongs to one of the oldest songs about the Magicians at the Tree, and it does not fit: a few lines about what the Magicians did, in an order that seems to matter, with words in them that nobody she has asked can explain. Aspen knew only half of it. An old woman on the lower paths knew a little more, and died last winter before Lyra could ask her again. Lyra does not know what it means, or whether it means anything at all. It has never occurred to her that the scholars at the Heart Tree might want to hear it. She thinks of songs as songs.

### What she wants and fears

Lyra wants every old song in the forest written down and sung, so that none of them ends with her. She fears that the old singers are going faster than she can find them, and that the verse that mattered most was lost with someone she did not reach in time.

A quest might ask a traveller to find an old singer in a distant village who might know the rest of a verse, to carry Lyra's book of songs to the Heart Tree, or simply to sit on the bridge outside the Dewdrop one evening and request a song nobody has asked for in years.
